content: Adhesive capsulitis, commonly referred to as frozen shoulder, is a frequent condition encountered in primary care settings. It can occur either as a primary condition or secondary to other underlying issues. A thorough clinical examination and accurate diagnosis are essential to distinguish it from other potential causes of shoulder pain and dysfunction. Below are the differential diagnoses for adhesive capsulitis: 1. Rotator Cuff Injury or Tendinopathy (with or without Supraspinatus Impingement): Patients often report a history of overuse or repetitive shoulder activity. Focal tenderness is present, but the passive range of motion is preserved. Diagnostic tests such as the Hawkins and Neer tests are typically positive in cases of impingement. 2. Rotator Cuff Tear: This condition is characterized by severe lateral arm pain and a limited range of both active and passive motion. The drop arm test is positive, and MRI is a valuable tool for confirming the diagnosis. 3. Acromioclavicular Arthropathy: Pain is localized to the superior aspect of the shoulder joint, often associated with a history of heavy weightlifting or repetitive overuse. The range of motion is preserved. Clinical diagnosis is supported by positive results on the cross-arm test and compression test. 4. Subacromial Bursitis: Diagnosis can be aided by the administration of a local lidocaine injection and confirmed with MRI imaging. 5. Cervical Radiculopathy or Cervical Disc Degeneration: Patients may present with weakness, numbness, and impaired light touch sensation in the upper extremity. These symptoms are often accompanied by a reduced active range of motion, particularly with neck movements. 6. Subdeltoid Bursitis: A history of overuse injury is common. MRI is helpful in confirming the diagnosis. 7. Tendinopathy of the Biceps at the Bicipital Groove: Patients typically report anterior upper arm pain. Positive results on the Speed and Yergason tests support the diagnosis. 8. Malignancy: Constitutional symptoms, such as weight loss or fatigue, and compressive symptoms from a Pancoast tumor should raise suspicion. Imaging studies are crucial to rule out frozen shoulder in such cases. 9. Polymyalgia Rheumatica: This condition is characterized by proximal muscle weakness in both the upper and lower extremities. An elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) can help differentiate it from adhesive capsulitis. 10. Autoimmune Diseases: Conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or rheumatoid arthritis, as well as other autoimmune disorders, may mimic the presentation of frozen shoulder.
